extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on evaluating whether claimed additional elements make a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, focusing on whether additional elements are well-understood/routine/conventional, constitute meaningful limitations, or are mere instructions to apply the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: (1) Being known in the art does not necessarily make an element conventional for §101 purposes—the novelty/obviousness inquiry is distinct (e.g., Enfish v. Microsoft shows known features can still be unconventional if they provide a technological improvement). (2) A factual determination is required to conclude an element is well-understood, routine, conventional (Berkheimer), but a prior-art search is not always necessary; examiners may rely on what courts or skilled artisans recognize as conventional in the field. The specification may itself indicate an element is conventional. An element should be treated as conventional only when the examiner can readily conclude, based on expertise, that it is widely prevalent or in common use in the relevant industry — similar to the analysis under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for what need not be described. Examples illustrate borderline situations (e.g., a glucose-sensing earring may be known to a few scientists but not routinely used in the field). (3) Combinations of conventional elements can nonetheless amount to an inventive concept if arranged non-conventionally (Diehr, Rapid Litigation Mgmt., BASCOM). Required written support: the factual determination must be expressly supported in writing (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)). Appropriate support includes: (a) citation to an express statement in the specification or applicant prosecution history indicating conventionality; (b) citation to relevant court decisions; (c) citation to publications showing conventionality; (d) a statement that the examiner is taking official notice of conventionality. If the examiner, relying on expertise, concludes additional elements do not amount to significantly more, a Step 2B rejection may be made; conversely, elements beyond those recognized as conventional will typically favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized well-understood computer functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain computer functions have been recognized by courts as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have treated as well-understood when recited generically: (i) receiving or transmitting data over a network (e.g., using the Internet to gather data, forwarding information via intermediary computer); (ii) performing repetitive calculations; (iii) electronic recordkeeping (creating/maintaining shadow accounts, updating activity logs); (iv) storing and retrieving information in memory; (v) electronically scanning or extracting data from a physical document (OCR); (vi) web browser back/forward functionality. Caveats: this listing is not exhaustive and does not mean all computer functions are conventional. Claims reciting only generic computer components performing generic computer functions may be ineligible if they amount to nothing more than implementation of an abstract idea, but generic components in combination can perform non-generic functions and be eligible (see DDR Holdings, BASCOM, Amdocs). Case citations: Symantec, TLI Communications, OIP Techs., buySAFE, DDR Holdings, Flook, Bancorp, Alice, Ultramercial, Versata, Content Extraction, Internet Patent Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized well-understood laboratory techniques (life sciences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain laboratory techniques in the life sciences have been treated by courts as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed at a high level of generality or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples the courts have recognized as conventional when claimed generically: (i) determining the level of a biomarker in blood by any means; (ii) using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) to amplify and detect DNA; (iii) detecting DNA or enzymes in a sample; (iv) immunizing a patient against a disease; (v) analyzing DNA for sequence information or allelic variants; (vi) freezing and thawing cells; (vii) amplifying and sequencing nucleic acid sequences; (viii) hybridizing a gene probe. Citations include Mayo, Cleveland Clinic Foundation v. True Health Diagnostics, Genetic Techs. v. Merial, Ariosa v. Sequenom, Classen, Rapid Litigation Mgmt., Ambry Genetics, University of Utah Research Foundation. As with computers, claiming these techniques at a high level of generality or as mere extra-solution activity can weigh against eligibility; context and how the technique is integrated into the claim matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have found well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have identified other non-technical activities as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed generically or as insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (i) recording a customer's order; (ii) shuffling and dealing a standard deck of cards; (iii) restricting public access to media by requiring viewing an advertisement; (iv) presenting offers and gathering statistics; (v) determining an estimated outcome and setting a price; (vi) arranging a hierarchy of groups, sorting information, eliminating less restrictive pricing information and determining the price. Case citations include Apple v. Ameranth, In re Smith, Ultramercial, OIP Techs., Versata. Examiners should consider these activities' level of generality and whether they are merely additional generic steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the judicial exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations are additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception or integrate the exception into a practical application. Considerations in MPEP § 2106.05(a)-(d) (e.g., improvement consideration, treatment/prophylaxis, insignificant extra-solution activity) can constitute meaningful limitations when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into practice. Examples: Diamond v. Diehr (use of Arrhenius equation integrated into an automated rubber-molding process — elements like installing rubber, closing the mold, measuring temperature, and automatically opening the press significantly limited and integrated the equation); Classen (analysis step combined with an immunization step integrated the abstract principle into a specific treatment); contrast Alice and OIP (additional elements that merely link to computers or involve routine data-gathering did not meaningfully limit the abstract idea). Examiners must evaluate additional elements both individually and in combination — elements that are not significant individually may be significant in combination (Diehr, BASCOM). Examiners may explain on the record why elements meaningfully limit the judicial exception. Overlap: treatment/prophylaxis considerations in Step 2A Prong Two may overlap with meaningful limitations (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application or recites significantly more only if additional elements do more than merely state the exception and add instructions to 'apply it' (or equivalent); merely instructing to implement an abstract idea on a generic computer is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court guidance: additional elements must do 'more than simply state the [judicial exception] while adding the words "apply it"' (Alice quoting Mayo). Examples: Mayo — measuring metabolite levels was routine and merely instructed application of the law of nature; Alice — recitation of a generic computer performing intermediated settlement was mere instruction to apply the abstract idea on a computer; Benson — converting BCD to binary had no meaningful practical application beyond computing. Requiring more than mere instructions does not mean the claim must be narrow; courts have found some broad claims eligible (McRO, Thales Visionix) and some narrow claims ineligible (Ultramercial, Electric Power Group). Examiners should beware analyses that turn on the draftsman's art and should look for specifics that meaningfully limit or integrate the exception rather than generic implementation steps.
